clue.text: Love story involving fine group as a possible compensation

definitions.note: an adverbial phrase standing for an adjective: describing something that could be set against a loss

indicators.note: something involving other things takes them inside itself, so the story wraps round what follows

parts.note: love is zero in tennis, shaped like the letter O
a fable is a short moral story
F is the pencil-grade abbreviation for fine
a set is a group of things belonging together

explanation.surface: A tale about a fine imposed on a group, told as a way of making amends.
explanation.walkthrough: Love is the tennis score, and the container sits one letter into the story, not at its edge.
explanation.definitionFit: Something offsetable can be balanced against a debt or loss, which is what a compensation does.

clue.text: Soften by kneading, careless when following mum

indicators.note: following tells us the word for careless is placed after the word for mum

parts.note: ma is a familiar word for mother
lax means slack or careless

explanation.surface: Someone gets sloppy kneading dough after their mother has shown them how.
explanation.definitionFit: Chambers gives malax as a rare verb meaning to make soft by working or kneading, as with plaster.

clue.text: Girl with pullover should keep mom's toddler happy

definitions.note: a cryptic description of the thing rather than a synonym

parts.note: baby is a familiar term for a girlfriend or girl
a jumper is the British word for a pullover sweater

explanation.surface: A girl in a sweater is supposed to keep a small child amused.
explanation.walkthrough: A baby-jumper is a harness on a spring frame in which a small child can bounce; 'mom' signals the American flavour of the device.
explanation.definitionFit: The harness lets a toddler bounce up and down for amusement, so it is described by its purpose of keeping the child content.

clue.text: Old convict: one with time doubled isn't common

parts.note: a, the indefinite article, means one
T is the abbreviation for time, written twice
ain't is the non-standard, vulgar form of isn't

explanation.surface: A former prisoner whose sentence was doubled is no ordinary criminal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Common' here means vulgar speech, so the colloquial contraction is wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: Attaint is an archaic verb meaning to convict or condemn under attainder, matching 'convict' as a verb.

clue.text: Snack bar's opening: cut piece from the press?

indicators.note: cut means trimmed, so the word that follows loses its end
an opening is the start of something, so only the first letter of that word is used

parts.note: the first letter of bar
an item is a piece in a newspaper

explanation.surface: A snack bar serving something cut from a newspaper, with a playful question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: A bite is a small amount of food, a light snack.

clue.text: Sweet wine Jock's beloved imbibes before pork

indicators.note: to imbibe is to drink in, so the beloved takes the following words inside

parts.note: jo is Scots for a sweetheart; Jock is a nickname for a Scot
ere is a poetic word for before
pork is the meat of a pig

explanation.surface: A Scotsman's sweetheart drinks sweet wine before her pork dinner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Before' looks like it only orders the pieces, but it supplies letters of its own as the poetic word for earlier.
explanation.definitionFit: Jerepigo is a heavy, sweet fortified wine, chiefly from South Africa.

clue.text: Clear passage through part of runs to pasture

indicators.note: part of says the answer is a portion of the following words' letters

parts.note: the letters straddle all three words, dropping the R and the ASTURE

explanation.surface: Animals run out to pasture once a passage is cleared.
explanation.definitionFit: To unstop is to remove a blockage, opening a way through.

clue.text: Versatile jazzman? He makes money, certainly

definitions.note: the question mark flags a definition by example

parts.note: M is the abbreviation for money
oke is a variant spelling of OK, meaning yes, certainly

explanation.surface: A jazz player who can turn his hand to anything is sure to earn money.
explanation.walkthrough: Commenters on the blog thought the definition a stretch; it works as an example, a jazzman being one kind of musician.
explanation.definitionFit: In old slang a moke was a performer who played several instruments, so a versatile jazz musician is one instance.

clue.text: Ancient homily on saint, most apt

parts.note: a prone was an old term for a homily or sermon
St is the abbreviation for saint

explanation.surface: An old sermon on a saint is judged the most fitting.
explanation.definitionFit: Prone can mean inclined or liable, so pronest is the superlative: the most apt or likely.

clue.text: Our diet needs adapting to become frivolous, à la française

indicators.note: adapting means altering, so these letters must be reworked

parts.note: the fodder, taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: Changing our diet is said to make us lighthearted in the French manner.
explanation.definitionFit: Étourdi is French for thoughtless or scatterbrained, borrowed into English; the phrase flags the French word.

clue.text: Rubber substitute causing uncontrollable movement in bearing

indicators.note: in says one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: face can mean appearance or bearing
a tic is an involuntary twitch

explanation.surface: A rubber substitute sets off an uncontrollable jerk in someone's posture.
explanation.definitionFit: Factice is a rubber-like material made by vulcanising vegetable oils, used to extend or replace rubber.

clue.text: Bridge player having void in hearts, capturing a third of tricks in turn

indicators.note: capturing means taking prisoner, so one piece holds the other inside

parts.note: a void in a bridge suit means none of it: no hearts, NO + H

indicators.note: turned round, the two letters of tricks run backwards

parts.note: the first two of its six letters

explanation.surface: A bridge player void in hearts still manages to take a share of the tricks.
explanation.definitionFit: North is one of the four compass positions at a bridge table, partnering South.

clue.text: Fragments machine repairer has left inside

indicators.note: to have is to hold, so the repairer's word holds something
inside says the short piece sits within the longer word

parts.note: a fitter assembles and repairs machinery
L is the abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: A mechanic has left fragments inside the machine.
explanation.definitionFit: Chambers lists flitters as fragments or tatters; flitter is the word for such a shred.

clue.text: The misguided need Dettol (nothing less), grasping one?

definitions.text: The misguided need Dettol (nothing less), grasping one?
definitions.note: the whole clue: the deluded think this harmless plant stings

indicators.note: grasping means holding inside, so the remaining letters take in one more
misguided means led astray, so the letters wander into a new order
less means minus, and nothing is the letter-shaped zero to be taken away

parts.note: the fodder, letter for letter
nothing is zero, shaped like O, removed from the fodder
a means one

explanation.surface: Fools who grab one think they will need antiseptic for the sting.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines too: a dead-nettle looks like a stinging nettle but does not sting, so only the misguided reach for Dettol, a British antiseptic.
explanation.definitionFit: Dead-nettle is a plant with nettle-like leaves that lacks stinging hairs, so grasping one is harmless.

clue.text: Native American chief, no more? It's a long story

indicators.note: no says the word that follows is to be absent from the longer one

parts.note: a sagamore was an Algonquian chief
taken as written, then removed

explanation.surface: A tribal chief has died; telling his life is a long story.
explanation.definitionFit: A saga is a long narrative, originally a Norse prose tale.

clue.text: Female prisoner, unruly teen put inside directly

indicators.note: put inside means placed within another word

parts.note: due means directly, as in due north

indicators.note: unruly means disorderly, so these letters are out of order

parts.note: the fodder, taken as written

explanation.surface: A rowdy teenage girl is locked up at once.
explanation.definitionFit: Détenue is the feminine form of détenu, a person held in custody, especially for political reasons.

clue.text: Dig up old — front of wording missing — battered 'RIP' follows

definitions.note: old marks the verb as obsolete

indicators.note: follows says the jumbled piece comes after the shortened word
points to the leading letter of the word that follows as the part concerned
missing means absent, so that leading letter is dropped

parts.note: text is the wording of a document

indicators.note: battered means knocked out of shape, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: the fodder, taken as written

explanation.surface: A gravestone's inscription, worn away at the front, reads a battered RIP.
explanation.definitionFit: Extirp is an obsolete form of extirpate, to root out or pull up by the roots.

clue.text: Pronounces oriental soup 'bum'

parts.note: pho is a Vietnamese noodle soup
nates is the anatomical word for the buttocks

explanation.surface: Someone declares an Asian soup rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bum' looks like slang for worthless, but it means the backside; in Britain bum is the everyday word for the bottom.
explanation.definitionFit: To phonate is to produce vocal sounds, so phonates means voices or utters.

clue.text: Timeless carouser, one Falstaff, say?

definitions.note: Falstaff is an example, flagged by say

indicators.note: timeless means without time, so the letter for time is dropped

parts.note: a toper is a heavy drinker
a means one

explanation.surface: Shakespeare's Falstaff is the eternal reveller.
explanation.walkthrough: Falstaff the drinker fits the surface, but the definition is Verdi's opera of that name.
explanation.definitionFit: Falstaff is the title of Verdi's last opera, so it is an example of the genre.

clue.text: Who isn't irritated by parking in conurbation?

indicators.note: irritated means stirred up, so the letters are shaken into a new order

parts.note: the fodder, letter for letter
P is the road-sign abbreviation for parking

explanation.surface: A rhetorical question: who in a big city is not annoyed by the parking?
explanation.definitionFit: A township is a town or urban settlement, a built-up area like a conurbation.

clue.text: By the way, more than half of strong drinks make you slash

indicators.note: more than half means only the larger front portion of the word survives, the tail dropped

parts.note: ob. abbreviates Latin obiter, by the way
liqueurs are strong sweet drinks; five of eight letters are kept

explanation.surface: Knocking back strong liqueurs makes you need the toilet.
explanation.walkthrough: In British slang a slash is a pee, the misleading surface sense. OB for obiter is in Chambers but rare.
explanation.definitionFit: An oblique is the typographic stroke /, also called a slash.

clue.text: He stitched cap with frills

indicators.note: frills are ruffled, gathered fabric, so the letters are ruffled too

parts.note: the fodder, letter for letter

explanation.surface: A man sewed a cap trimmed with frills.
explanation.definitionFit: Whipcat is an old contemptuous name for a tailor, a man whose trade is stitching.

clue.text: What could make me a lord?

definitions.text: What could make me a lord?
definitions.note: the whole clue: the rank that would ennoble the speaker

indicators.note: asks what could be made from these letters, inviting a rearrangement

parts.note: the fodder, letter for letter

explanation.surface: A commoner wonders aloud what honour would raise them to the peerage.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the anagram and the definition: being raised to an earldom would make the speaker a peer.
explanation.definitionFit: An earldom is the rank of an earl, a British title of nobility whose holder is styled Lord.

clue.text: Form of argot a semi-polyglot rubbished and binned?

indicators.note: binned means put into a bin, placing the jumble inside

parts.note: the bin is suggested by the word itself

indicators.note: rubbished means trashed, so the letters are scrambled
semi means half, so the front half of the word is dropped

parts.note: taken as written
a polyglot speaks many languages; only its back half is kept

explanation.surface: A linguist dismisses a kind of slang and throws it away.
explanation.walkthrough: Bog Latin is a name for Shelta, an Irish travellers' cant, or for mock Latin.
explanation.definitionFit: Bog Latin is a secret jargon or cant, the kind of in-group language argot means.

clue.text: You require a horn or buzzer for each

definitions.note: loose: the thing you need when a hooter is called for

parts.note: a bee buzzes
per means for each, as in per head

explanation.surface: Each person must carry a horn or buzzer, perhaps for a race start.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is loose: a beeper is any device sounding a warning tone, like a horn.
explanation.definitionFit: A beeper is a device that emits a short warning tone, used as a signal in place of a horn.

clue.text: Old poet's immediately energized after book

indicators.note: after places the word for energized behind the abbreviation for book

parts.note: B is the abbreviation for book
a live wire is energized, carrying current

explanation.surface: An old poet suddenly comes alive after reading a book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old poet's' marks a word used by Spenser and older writers.
explanation.definitionFit: Blive is a Spenserian form of belive, meaning at once or soon.

clue.text: Sweet Rosie's cut short English in old Scottish exam (6, two words)

indicators.note: cut short means losing the end, so the final letter goes

parts.note: Sweet Rosie O'Grady is an 1896 popular song
E is the abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: A girl named Rosie fails to finish her English paper in an old Scottish exam.
explanation.definitionFit: The O Grade, Ordinary Grade, was the Scottish school exam taken at about sixteen, replaced in the late 1980s.

clue.text: Cook making case for exotic bird or tropical fish

indicators.note: to make a case for something is to enclose it, so one word wraps the other

parts.note: to do food is to cook it
the ani is a tropical American cuckoo

explanation.surface: A chef argues for serving an exotic bird or a tropical fish.
explanation.definitionFit: A danio is a small brightly striped freshwater fish of the carp family, such as the zebra danio of aquariums.

clue.text: Grasp without hearing lecturer repaid toiling

parts.note: L is the abbreviation for lecturer

indicators.note: toiling means labouring, as if the letters are worked over into a new shape

parts.note: the fodder, taken as written

explanation.surface: A lecturer paid back for hard labour still cannot follow what is said.
explanation.definitionFit: To lip-read is to understand speech by watching the speaker's mouth, without hearing the sound.

clue.text: Indication of lung disease? MO lost confidence

indicators.note: something lost is gone, so those letters are taken away

parts.note: morale is confidence or spirit
taken as written, then removed

explanation.surface: A medical officer loses confidence over a sign of lung disease.
explanation.walkthrough: MO looks like the medical officer of the surface; it is simply the two letters dropped from the front.
explanation.definitionFit: A rale is a rattling sound heard in diseased lungs through a stethoscope.

clue.text: Formerly straight, slewed by the sound of it

definitions.note: straight in the sense of straightaway

indicators.note: says the word is identified by how it is spoken, not spelt

parts.note: slewed is slang for drunk

explanation.surface: Something once straight has twisted round, it seems.
explanation.walkthrough: Slewed looks like twisted but is slang for drunk, as is tight.
explanation.definitionFit: Tite is an obsolete adverb meaning promptly or at once, as straight means immediately.

clue.text: It keeps mill-wheel turning — hindrance restricts one

indicators.note: to restrict is to hem in, so one word encloses the other

parts.note: a let is a hindrance, as in without let or hindrance
a means one

explanation.surface: Something keeps a mill-wheel going though an obstacle holds it back.
explanation.definitionFit: A leat is an open channel bringing water to a mill, which drives its wheel.

clue.text: Free camping? Sort of fork provided

indicators.note: camping means being under canvas, so a word is put inside the shelter

parts.note: campers sleep in a tent
to rid is to free

explanation.surface: A free campsite even provides some kind of fork.
explanation.definitionFit: A trident is a three-pronged spear, a large fork like Neptune's.

clue.text: Property of the same value, first to last

indicators.note: the first letter is moved round to the end

parts.note: equal means of the same value

explanation.surface: Two properties are worth the same, from first to last.
explanation.definitionFit: In philosophy a quale is a quality or property considered on its own, as experienced.

clue.text: Upmarket resort, rooms in ——? Torremolinos is wrong

indicators.note: wrong means incorrect, so the letters are out of their right order

parts.note: the fodder, letter for letter
taken as written, then subtracted from the jumble

explanation.surface: Someone corrects a brochure: the smart rooms are not in Torremolinos.
explanation.walkthrough: A composite anagram: the letters of TORREMOLINOS IS rearrange to ROOMS IN plus the answer, which fills the dash. Torremolinos is a Spanish package-holiday resort.
explanation.definitionFit: Estoril is a fashionable seaside resort on the Portuguese Riviera near Lisbon.

clue.text: After workout, short, old uncle goes for a wine

indicators.note: after places the remaining pieces behind the word for workout

parts.note: PE is physical education, a school workout
terse means short or curt
eme is an old word for an uncle

explanation.surface: After exercise, a short elderly uncle goes off for a glass of wine.
explanation.definitionFit: Peter-see-me is an old name for a Spanish wine, a corruption of Pedro Ximénez.
